q: Binary variables $x_1,\dots,x_4$. Compare the aggregated constraint $\tfrac13(x_1+x_2+x_3)\le x_4$ with the disaggregated system $x_1\le x_4$, $x_2\le x_4$, $x_3\le x_4$. In the LP relaxation ($0\le x\le1$), minimise $x_4$ subject to $x_1=1$ and the aggregated constraint. What is the optimal value?
explain: With $x_1=1$ and $x_2=x_3=0$ the aggregated row only requires $x_4\ge\tfrac13$. The disaggregated system gives $x_4\ge x_1=1$, the integer answer. Summing the three disaggregated inequalities and dividing by 3 yields the aggregated one, so the disaggregated relaxation is contained in the aggregated relaxation and its bounds are at least as good; the two systems have the same integer solutions. (Worked for this bank; the source is a question paper.)

q: A MILP with exactly one integer variable $x$ (all other variables continuous) is solved by LP-based branch-and-bound; every feasible LP relaxation has a unique optimal solution. Show that the tree has at most three nodes.
model:
If the root LP optimum $r$ has an integer value $x_r=v$, the tree has one node. Otherwise branch: left child $x\le\lfloor v\rfloor$, right child $x\ge\lceil v\rceil$.
Claim: a feasible child attains its LP optimum on the new bound. Take the left child, with optimum $p$, and suppose $x_p \lt\lfloor v\rfloor$. The root is a relaxation of the child, so $r$ is at least as good as $p$. The segment from $p$ to $r$ lies in the feasible region of the root LP (convexity) and crosses the hyperplane $x=\lfloor v\rfloor$ at a point $q\ne p$, which is feasible for the left child. The objective is linear, so its value at $q$ lies between the values at $p$ and $r$: $q$ is at least as good as $p$, contradicting the uniqueness of the child's optimum. Hence $x_p=\lfloor v\rfloor$, an integer, and the left child is a leaf (integral, or infeasible). The same argument works for the right child with $\lceil v\rceil$. So there are at most $1+2=3$ nodes.
rubric: One node if the root solution is integral; otherwise two children $x\le\lfloor v\rfloor$ and $x\ge\lceil v\rceil$
Convexity: the segment between the child's optimum and the root optimum crosses the branching bound
Linearity of the objective and uniqueness give a contradiction unless the child's optimum lies on the bound
Concludes that both children are leaves: at most 3 nodes
explain: With a single integer variable, one branching is always enough; the difficulty of MILP comes from the interaction of several integer variables. (The source is a question paper; this solution was worked for the bank.)

q: State the classical sufficient condition for a matrix $A$ to be totally unimodular (at most two nonzeros per column, partition of the rows), with the idea of its proof.
a:
$A$ is TU if
  1. every entry is $0$, $+1$ or $-1$;
  2. every column has at most two nonzero entries;
  3. the rows can be partitioned into $M_1$ and $M_2$ such that, for every column with two nonzeros, the sum of its entries in $M_1$ equals the sum of its entries in $M_2$ (two entries of the same sign lie in different classes, two entries of opposite sign in the same class).
Proof idea: take a smallest square submatrix $B$ with $\det B\notin\{0,\pm1\}$. It has no zero column and no column with a single nonzero (expanding along it would give a smaller bad submatrix), so every column of $B$ has two nonzeros. By (3) the rows of $B$ in $M_1$ and those in $M_2$ have the same sum, so the rows are linearly dependent and $\det B=0$: a contradiction.

explain: The condition covers node–arc incidence matrices of directed graphs ($M_2=\emptyset$) and incidence matrices of bipartite graphs ($M_1,M_2$ = the two sides).

q: What is the link between total unimodularity of an integer matrix $A$ and integrality of the polyhedra $\{x : Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}$?
a: For an integer matrix $A$: the polyhedron $\{x: Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}$ is integral for every integer vector $b$ if and only if $A$ is totally unimodular. Moreover, if $A$ is TU and $b$ is integer, $\{x:Ax\le b\}$ coincides with its integer hull, so the LP relaxation solves the integer program.

q: Show that the polyhedron $P=\{(x_1,\dots,x_m,y)\ge0 : y\le1,\ x_i\le y\ \text{for } i=1,\dots,m\}$ is integral.
model: Write $P=\{z\ge0 : Mz\le b\}$ with $z=(x,y)$, where $M$ has the $m$ rows $e_i-e_y$ (for $x_i-y\le0$) and the row $e_y$ (for $y\le1$), and $b=(0,\dots,0,1)$. Every row of $M$ has at most one $+1$ and at most one $-1$. Hence every column of $M^\top$ has at most two nonzeros and, when it has two, they are a $+1$ and a $-1$: the sufficient condition for total unimodularity holds with all rows in one class. So $M^\top$ is TU, and therefore $M$ is TU. Since $b$ is integer, $\{z\ge0 : Mz\le b\}$ is integral (TU matrix with integer right-hand side).
rubric: Writes the constraint matrix: rows $e_i-e_y$ and $e_y$
Observes at most one $+1$ and one $-1$ per row (the transpose is a directed incidence-type matrix)
Concludes that $M$ is TU (via $M^\top$)
Integer right-hand side and TU matrix give an integral polyhedron
explain: $P$ is the LP relaxation of the linking constraints "a client can be served only if the facility is open" for one facility, which explains why the disaggregated constraints $x_i\le y$ are ideal for this piece of a model. (The lecture gives no solution; this one was worked for the bank and checked by brute force for $m=3$.)

q: State the Ghouila-Houri characterisation of totally unimodular matrices and its corollary for matrices with at most two nonzeros per column.
a: $A$ is TU if and only if every subset $I$ of its rows can be split into two parts $K$ and $L$ such that, for every column $j$, $$\Big|\sum_{i\in K}a_{ij}-\sum_{i\in L}a_{ij}\Big|\le1 .$$ Corollary: $A$ is TU if every column has at most two nonzeros, each equal to $\pm1$, and the columns with two nonzeros sum to 0 (one $+1$ and one $-1$), as in the node–arc incidence matrix of a directed graph.

source.label: Brown University CS 149 (Intro to Combinatorial Optimization) — slides "Integer Programming: Total Unimodularity"

explain: Typical use: for a 0/1 matrix whose ones are consecutive in every column, sort the selected rows and put them alternately in $K$ and $L$; in each column the selected ones are consecutive, so the alternating sum is $-1$, $0$ or $1$.

q: Which operations preserve total unimodularity?
a: If $A$ is TU, then so are: $A^\top$; $(A\ \ I)$; $(A\ \ {-A})$; $A^{-1}$ when $A$ is square and nonsingular; and every matrix obtained from $A$ by deleting or duplicating a row or column, multiplying a row or column by $-1$, permuting rows or columns, or pivoting.

q: $S=\{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{Z}^2_+ : x_1\le5,\ x_1-4x_2\le0\}$, and $x^*=(5,\tfrac54)$ is a fractional vertex of its LP relaxation. With the multipliers $u=(\tfrac34,\tfrac14)$ on the two constraints, which Chvátal–Gomory cut is obtained?
explain: $\tfrac34\,(x_1\le5)+\tfrac14\,(x_1-4x_2\le0)$ gives $x_1-x_2\le\tfrac{15}{4}$; the left-hand side has integer coefficients, so the right-hand side is rounded down: $x_1-x_2\le3$. At $x^*$: $5-1.25=3.75 \gt 3$, so $x^*$ is cut off. Validity check: $x_1=5$ needs $x_2\ge2$ and $1\le x_1\le4$ needs $x_2\ge1$, so $x_1-x_2\le3$ on $S$. The unrounded combination does not cut $x^*$, and rounding up to 4 is pointless. (Worked for this bank; the source has no solutions.)

q: $S=\{x\in\{0,1\}^3 : x_1+x_2-2x_3\le0\}$. The point $(1,0,\tfrac12)$ belongs to the LP relaxation. Derive a Chvátal–Gomory cut that cuts it off, and interpret the cut.
model: Take the multiplier $\tfrac12$ on each of $x_1+x_2-2x_3\le0$, $-x_2\le0$ and $x_1\le1$: the sum is $x_1-x_3\le\tfrac12$. The left-hand side has integer coefficients, so round the right-hand side down: $$x_1-x_3\le0,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad x_1\le x_3 .$$ At the point $(1,0,\tfrac12)$: $1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12 \gt 0$, so it is cut off. Interpretation: $x_1=1$ forces $x_3=1$; by symmetry $x_2\le x_3$ is valid as well. These are the disaggregated versions of the aggregated row $x_1+x_2\le2x_3$.
rubric: Nonnegative combination of the constraint with $-x_2\le0$ and $x_1\le1$ (multipliers $\tfrac12$)
Obtains $x_1-x_3\le\tfrac12$
Rounds down to $x_1-x_3\le0$
Checks that the point violates the cut, or states the logical meaning $x_1=1\Rightarrow x_3=1$
explain: The example shows that the strong (disaggregated) linking constraints are rank-1 Chvátal–Gomory cuts of the weak (aggregated) formulation. (Worked for this bank; the source has no solutions.)

q: $S=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^4_+ : 4x_1+8x_2+7x_3+5x_4\le33\}$. Which Chvátal–Gomory cut is obtained with the multiplier $u=\tfrac17$, and does it cut off the LP vertex $(0,0,\tfrac{33}{7},0)$?
explain: $\lfloor\tfrac47\rfloor=0$, $\lfloor\tfrac87\rfloor=1$, $\lfloor\tfrac77\rfloor=1$, $\lfloor\tfrac57\rfloor=0$ and $\lfloor\tfrac{33}{7}\rfloor=4$, so the cut is $x_2+x_3\le4$. The vertex has $x_3=\tfrac{33}{7}\approx4.71 \gt 4$ and is removed. Rounding the coefficients up instead gives the invalid $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4\le4$ ($x_1=8$ is feasible); rounding the right-hand side up gives nothing; $x_3\le4$ is valid but weaker, because it drops the coefficient $\lfloor\tfrac87\rfloor=1$ of $x_2$. (Worked for this bank; the source has no solutions.)

q: $\max 4x_1-6x_2$ s.t. $x_1+x_2\le5$, $2x_1-3x_2\le1$, $x\ge0$ integer. The LP relaxation has optimal value 2, attained on the whole edge from $(\tfrac12,0)$ to $(\tfrac{16}{5},\tfrac95)$. Which Chvátal–Gomory cut results from the multipliers $u=(\tfrac35,\tfrac15)$ on the two constraints, and what does it do?
options: $x_1\le3$: it cuts off the vertex $(\tfrac{16}{5},\tfrac95)$ and no integer feasible point
explain: $\tfrac35(x_1+x_2)+\tfrac15(2x_1-3x_2)=x_1$ and $\tfrac35\cdot5+\tfrac15\cdot1=\tfrac{16}{5}$, so the combination is $x_1\le\tfrac{16}{5}$, rounded down to $x_1\le3$. It removes $(3.2,1.8)$ but not $(\tfrac12,0)$; that vertex is removed by another Chvátal–Gomory cut, $x_1-2x_2\le0$ (multipliers $\tfrac12$ on $2x_1-3x_2\le1$ and on $-x_2\le0$). The objective is twice the left-hand side of the second constraint, which explains the LP value 2 on the whole edge; the integer point $(2,1)$ lies on that edge, so the integer optimum is also 2. (Worked for this bank; the source has no solutions.)

q: Let $n$ be odd and consider $$\min x_{n+1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad2x_1+2x_2+\dots+2x_n+x_{n+1}=n,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^{n+1}.$$ Show that LP-based branch-and-bound (branching on variables, no cutting planes) must explore at least $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ nodes.
model:
Optimal value. $n$ is odd and $2\sum_ix_i$ is even, so every integer solution has $x_{n+1}=1$: $z^*=1$.
Nodes that cannot be pruned. Consider a node in which $k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ are fixed, $j$ of them to 1, and $x_{n+1}$ is free or fixed to 0. With $x_{n+1}=0$ the $n-k$ free variables must sum to $(n-2j)/2$, which is possible with values in $[0,1]$ because $n-2j\ge0$ (as $j\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$) and $n-2j\le2(n-k)$ (as $k-j\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$). So the LP of the node is feasible with value $0 \lt 1$: the node is pruned neither by infeasibility nor by bound. Its LP solution cannot be integral, since an integral point with $x_{n+1}=0$ would make the even number $2\sum_ix_i$ equal to the odd number $n$. Hence the node must be branched.
Counting. By induction, the subtree of such a node with $k$ fixed variables contains at least $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor-k}$ nodes: branching on some $x_i$ gives two children with $k+1$ fixed variables, and branching on $x_{n+1}$ gives the child $x_{n+1}=0$ with the same $k$, which must be branched again. For the root ($k=0$) this gives at least $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ nodes.
rubric: Parity argument: every integer solution has $x_{n+1}=1$, so $z^*=1$
Shows that the LP at a node with at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ fixed $x$-variables is feasible with value 0
Shows that this LP solution cannot be integral, so the node is pruned neither by bound nor by integrality
Concludes that all nodes down to depth $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ are created: at least $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ nodes
explain: The LP bound stays at 0 until more than half of the variables are fixed, so bounding never helps, whereas a single Chvátal–Gomory cut ($\sum_ix_i\le(n-1)/2$, which implies $x_{n+1}\ge1$) closes the gap at the root. A small LP-based branch-and-bound written to check this needed 11, 39, 139 and 503 nodes for $n=3,5,7,9$. (The source is a question sheet; this solution was worked for the bank.)
